source_document.body:
Businesses spend an estimated $1.54 million a year on manual procurement and supply chain work that AI could automate , according to a new Ivalua report. Yet just 34% of organizations surveyed have put AI into production in procurement.
What’s Related
The report found that 86% of organizations are deploying, piloting, or considering AI in procurement. Among organizations already using AI, 69% said they have seen a return on their investment.
The findings also show the way teams spend their time is changing. Some 72% of AI adopters said the technology has increased the time available for strategy and building supplier relationships.
RELATED STORIES: AI Is Reshaping Procurement Jobs, But Few Leaders Have Changed Them | Why Procurement Teams Need Rules Before Giving AI More Power
The cost of waiting
The dollar figure comes from two survey findings: average annual spending of $8.29 million on procurement and supply chain staff, and an average of 18.6% of team time spent on manual tasks respondents said could be automated or handled by AI. Multiplying those figures produces an estimated annual labor cost of approximately $1.54 million per organization.
That calculation estimates the staff time spent on those tasks. It does not measure cash savings companies have achieved by introducing AI, and the amount each organization could save would depend on its staffing costs and the work it automates.
“The cost of waiting is becoming harder to ignore,” said Paul Zammit, AI GTM Lead at Ivalua. “Organizations that have taken AI into production are already seeing returns, while those stuck in pilot mode are paying twice: millions spent on manual work, and strategic ground conceded to faster-moving competitors.”
Data problems slow adoption
Half of respondents said their procurement data is not reliable enough to produce meaningful AI insights. Nearly half (45%) said information sits in four or more separate systems, making it harder to build a complete picture of purchasing and suppliers.
Meanwhile, 51% of procurement leaders said their teams trail other business functions in AI adoption. Sapio Research conducted the survey in March 2026, including 800 procurement decision-makers and 200 CIOs, evenly split across four countries.
“The organizations seeing the greatest gains aren't simply those investing in AI, but those putting the right data foundations in place to make it useful,” Zammit said.
